common_name: Early White Bush Scallop Squash (Classic White Patty Pan Squash)

planting.note: Direct sow after the last frost once soil has warmed, spacing hills to give the bushy plants room to spread.

directions: This is one of the oldest American summer squash types, grown by colonial gardeners well before it was formally selected and named in the 19th century, producing the classic ivory-white, scallop-edged flying-saucer fruit. Harvest at 2-3 inches across while the rind is still soft enough to pierce with a fingernail; older fruit turns starchy and tough quickly. The compact bush habit suits small beds and containers better than vining winter squash, and steady picking every couple of days keeps the plant setting new fruit through the season. Its pale color and mild, delicate flavor make it a good choice for gardeners wanting a change from the more common yellow and green scallop types.

common_name: Cash Flow Hybrid Zucchini (High-Yield Market Zucchini)

planting.note: Direct sow once soil has warmed after last frost, or start indoors 2-3 weeks early for a jump on the season.

directions: Cash Flow was bred as a market-grower's zucchini, prized for setting an unusually high number of straight, uniform dark-green fruit in quick succession from an open, easy-to-harvest plant. Pick fruit small, at 6-8 inches, for the best texture and to keep the vigorous plant cranking out more; a single well-fed plant can produce for weeks with regular harvest. The open habit makes fruit easy to spot under the leaves, cutting down on the oversized zucchini that hide until harvest day. A dependable choice for gardeners who want a steady, heavy zucchini harvest without much fuss.

planting.note: Direct sow or transplant after all frost danger has passed and soil has warmed well into the 70s.

directions: Sugar Nut is a personal-size muskmelon bred for small households and small gardens, producing heavily netted, orange-fleshed fruit that average just under 2 pounds so a single melon serves one or two people without waste. Its compact vines and shorter internodes let it perform well in raised beds and large containers compared with sprawling standard cantaloupe types. High sugar content and a small seed cavity give a favorable flesh-to-seed ratio for its size, and its early maturity suits gardeners in shorter-season regions who struggle to ripen full-size cantaloupe. Vine to a trellis or let it sprawl, keeping fruit off wet soil to prevent rot.

common_name: President Hybrid Zucchini (AAS-Winning Classic Green Zucchini)

planting.note: Direct sow after the last frost into warm, fertile soil, or transplant young seedlings started 2-3 weeks earlier indoors.

directions: President was one of the first hybrid zucchinis to combine early vigor with a long, productive harvest window, and it remains a benchmark against which newer hybrid zucchinis are still compared. The upright, semi-open plant carries glossy, dark green, cylindrical fruit that stay tender even a bit past the ideal 6-8 inch harvest size, giving gardeners more forgiveness than many modern types. Its reliable, heavy set makes it a solid choice for gardeners who just want zucchini without babying a temperamental variety. Keep fruit picked regularly to prevent the plant from slowing production.

planting.note: Direct sow or transplant after soil has warmed well past 70°F, since honeydew is slower to establish than cantaloupe.

directions: Earlidew was developed to bring honeydew melon within reach of gardeners in shorter, cooler growing seasons where standard honeydew varieties often fail to ripen before fall. It produces smooth, pale green-white rinds around sweet, light green flesh on vines noticeably more compact than typical honeydew types. Because honeydew does not slip from the vine at maturity the way cantaloupe does, watch for the blossom end to soften slightly and the rind to take on a faint yellow cast as ripeness cues. Its earlier maturity window makes it one of the more practical honeydew choices for northern vegetable gardens.

planting.note: Direct sow after all frost danger has passed, giving the long rampant vines plenty of room or a sturdy trellis to climb.

directions: Tahitian Melon Squash grows a huge, pale blue-green, club-shaped fruit that can reach 2 feet long and 20-plus pounds, with dense, deep orange flesh notably lower in fiber and sweeter than most butternut types, closer in eating quality to a sweet potato. The extremely long, vigorous vines need generous space or a strong trellis to support the developing fruit off the ground. Despite its huge size, a single fruit stores well for months and yields a lot of smooth, easily pureed flesh for soups and baking. A conversation-piece squash for gardeners with room to let vines ramble and a taste for very sweet, low-fiber winter squash.
sources: University of Hawaii College of Tropical Agriculture and Human Resources
